title: One-pointed practice removes them (1.32)
hook: nine obstacles, and Patanjali's remedy fits in one short sutra: practice on one thing

segments.voice: Yesterday: the nine obstacles, antaraya, not demons, just Tuesday. Illness, dullness, doubt, carelessness, laziness, craving, false seeing, plateaus, slipping. Which one did you catch by name? Today, the remedy. Day four hundred thirty-nine.

A man needs water. He digs ten feet down in one corner of his field, finds only dry dirt, and gives up. He digs ten feet somewhere else. Dry again. By the end of the summer the field is full of shallow holes, and he's still carrying water up from the river. One hole, dug forty feet down, would have reached it. Yesterday Patanjali named nine obstacles. You might expect nine cures. He gives one, in a single short sutra, and it's that one deep hole: one thing.
screen: `TEN SHALLOW HOLES, NO WATER.` → `ONE HOLE, DUG DEEP.` → `NINE OBSTACLES, ONE REMEDY.`

segments.voice: Sutra 1.32: tat pratishedhartham eka tattva abhyasah. To prevent them, practice on one principle. Tat, them: the obstacles. Pratishedha: keeping away, warding off. Eka: one. Tattva: a principle, a reality, literally thatness. Abhyasa: practice, the same word from five days ago, the steady return. So: to keep the scatterings away, return again and again to one thing. What is the one thing? Here the commentators part ways, and the sutra itself doesn't say. Vyasa reads it as any single object the mind is fixed on, one support instead of many. Others point to the sutras just before, about Ishvara and om, and read the one principle as the Lord. Both readings share the same shape: stop spreading out. The obstacles feed on scattering. Doubt grows when you keep switching methods. Laziness grows when nothing is the main thing. Plateaus feel endless when you keep starting over somewhere new. Vyasa also describes a mind that is one-pointed, ekagra, focused on a single object, and he treats it as the ground where real absorption becomes possible. That's where the word one-pointed in today's title comes from. Notice how modest this is. Not one perfect thing. Not the right thing. Just one thing, chosen and returned to. The next sutras, starting tomorrow, offer a list of possible one things. But today's teaching is simply the rule underneath them: pick one, and stay.
screen: `EKA TATTVA: ONE PRINCIPLE.` · `WHAT IS THE ONE THING?` · `OBSTACLES FEED ON SCATTERING.` · then, large: `PICK ONE, AND STAY.`

segments.voice: Before the bell, choose your one thing for this sit. The breath at the nostrils, a word like om, or the feeling of your hands resting. Just one. Now sit with it. Every time the mind offers you a second thing, a better object, a plan, a different technique, let it go and return to the one you chose. Don't switch, even if another seems more interesting. One thing, all the way to the bell. The bell holds the time.
Ekagra, one-pointed, a mind fixed on a single object. Sutra 1.32: to keep the obstacles away, practice on one principle, returning again and again to a single thing.
Your line: one thing. For one hour today, close every tab but one, literal or not, and give that one thing your full return, again and again. Day four hundred thirty-nine.

howItsDone: Many Hindu teachers advise choosing one practice, one mantra or one form of the divine and staying with it for years, rather than switching methods, and they often cite Yoga Sutra 1.32 for this.

pairs: one-pointed: a mind on a single object

myth: Patanjali gives a separate cure for each of the nine obstacles
sutra 1.32 gives one remedy: practice on one principle.
commentators disagree about what the one principle is
Vyasa reads any single object; others read it as Ishvara, from the sutras just before.
the word abhyasa in 1.32 is the same practice word from 1.12
the steady return, paired earlier with non-attachment.

fork.setup: your meditation feels stuck, and you find three new techniques online. what does sutra 1.32 suggest?
options: pick one thing and keep returning to it.
fork.reveal: to ward off the obstacles, practice on one principle. switching keeps the mind scattered, which is what the obstacles feed on.

original.note: Sanskrit ekāgra: one-pointed, a mind fixed on a single object. Vyasa's term; the source of 'one-pointed'.

trapdoor: what you thought: one-pointed means intense concentration, forcing the mind still.
what it means: choosing one thing and returning to it, again and again, so the scattering has nothing to feed on.
what a scholar hears: Vyasa reads eka-tattva as a single object; other commentators read it as Ishvara, given 1.23–1.29; ekagra is one of Vyasa's five states of mind.

sources.ref: Yoga Sutras of Patanjali 1.32 (practice on one principle)
Vyasa, Yoga Bhashya on 1.1 and 1.32 (ekagra, the one-pointed mind)

notes: The index word is 'One-pointed practice removes them' (title head cut short); kept exactly. The word segment says the full title. Suggest the outline use 'eka tattva' or 'one-pointed'.
Which commentators read eka-tattva as Ishvara (e.g. Vachaspati Mishra) should be confirmed; kept general as 'others'.
Vyasa's five states of mind (kshipta, mudha, vikshipta, ekagra, niruddha) appear in his comment on 1.1.
